title: How to optimize a game
author: obviousBee87
selftext:
I made a "space trucking" game where the cargo is the enemy. You tow stuff on a stretchy rope in zero gravity, and every time you brake or turn, the load swings or sloshes and tries to drag you into a wall. 

It's a fun little physics, 2.5D sparge game, but I have a problem: the game uses a bit too much RAM imo. When running it in browser (it's on itch.io), it can go up to 2Gb.

So I need some advice on how to optimize it. Also, let me know if you want to try the game, I can post the link in comments.

comments.author: imlo2
comments.body: Do just the same as in traditional development; start profiling it and don't try to guess what takes time in your update for each frame. Then eventually the resource-consuming things get revealed, and you can start to think about a strategy to minimize the cost and how to optimize. Often it's a combination of many small things, but sometimes it's a huge resource hog or two. Your agent can do all of these things very well, and both Codex and Claude can produce well (and often even without prompting) good interpretations and visualizations of such things, so you can get the output on a level you can understand.

comments.author: ledniv
comments.body:
If RAM is the problem, I would specifically ask the agent to help you profile **memory usage**, not just “optimize the game.” Those are very different problems.

Take a memory snapshot after loading the game, then another after playing for a while, and compare them. You want to know what is actually consuming the 2 GB. It could be textures, audio, duplicated assets, physics objects, objects that are never released, or runtime allocations that keep accumulating. If memory keeps growing while you play, that is especially useful because it may point to something being created repeatedly and never freed.

For gameplay data, I also try to avoid creating lots of little runtime objects. Keeping frequently used state in arrays, reusing objects through pools, and explicitly controlling when memory is allocated and released can make memory behavior much more predictable. But I would profile first rather than asking the AI to blindly rewrite things.

I made a free Data Oriented Design skill for coding agents that includes a lot of these rules around data layout, allocations, pooling, and performance:

[https://github.com/Data-Oriented-Design-for-Games/data-oriented-design](https://github.com/Data-Oriented-Design-for-Games/data-oriented-design)

Small plug: I also cover memory layout, allocations, pooling, profiling, and how those decisions affect performance in *High Performance Unity Game Development with Data Oriented Design*. Despite Unity being in the title, a lot of the underlying material applies to other engines too.

[https://www.manning.com/books/high-performance-unity-game-development](https://www.manning.com/books/high-performance-unity-game-development)

comments.author: OWazabi
comments.body:
Feels like brainstorming this with your agent is the best way to do it regardless.
Just have him stress test and audit everything, keep logs etc, then reflect on the different layers of improvement and various optimizations that can be don, and let him implement/test the most relevant ones
